Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Predicting Surface Displacement Fields of Laser Powder Bed Fusion Parts Using STL-Derived Graphs and Part-Level Descriptors
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Predicting part distortion before fabrication remains challenging in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), while thermomechanical simulation is computationally expensive for repeated design evaluations. This study presents a two-branch graph attention network (GAT) to predict three-dimensional surface displacement directly from STL-derived graphs. The first branch learns geometric relationships among connected vertices of a densified STL surface mesh, while the second incorporates 12 part-level descriptors of mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape. Displacement labels from ANSYS Additive Print simulations are mapped onto STL vertices using Gaussian-kernel weighted averaging. Evaluated on 117 parts using five-fold cross-validation split by part, the model achieves an R^2 of 0.946 and a mean absolute error of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude. Relative to a node-wise multilayer perceptron, GAT improves R^2 from 0.913 to 0.946; for build-direction displacement, R^2 increases from 0.903 to 0.939. GAT also outperforms GraphSAGE (R^2 = 0.936) and a graph convolutional network (R^2 = 0.934) across all five folds. Ablation experiments show that removing mass-distribution descriptors reduces magnitude R^2 to 0.900, while removing build-plate contact and overhang descriptors reduces it to 0.920. These results demonstrate the value of combining local mesh connectivity with global geometric descriptors to predict LPBF distortion, enabling faster design iteration and earlier identification of distortion-prone geometries.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to propose statistical models, but these systems struggle on challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents), a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating reusable diagnostic tools. We evaluate VESTA using three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers that culminates in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines for statistical analysis and visual tool creation, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. Against strong agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode), VESTA is better on all time series tasks and on complex distribution fitting tasks, though the harnesses achieve better fits on simpler distributions. Further, dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VESTA VLM critic can reason over directly.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Scalable fault vulnerability analysis for ReRAM-based process-in-memory CNN accelerators
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector multiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (\textit{SaH}) and stuck-at-low (\textit{SaL}) resistance states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accuracy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and measuring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate, it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerability at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our proposed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks, whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about $10^4\times-10^5\times$, enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only a few minutes or hours.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: A human-in-the-loop Bayesian optimization framework for constraint-aware bioprocess development
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: We present Pareto Front Guided Sampling (PFGS), a human-in-the-loop (HiL) Bayesian Optimization (BO) framework that reformulates surrogate-model predictions as a multi-objective optimization problem, allowing domain knowledge to beadded intuitively to any BO problem. PFGS addresses constrained optimization by treating the posterior probability of constraint satisfaction as an explicit Pareto objective, and robust optimization via a Monte Carlo estimate of expected lower-confidence performance under input perturbations, capturing likely degradation. The multi-dimensional Pareto front makes trade-offs between predicted performance, model uncertainty, constraint satisfaction, and robustness visible through pairwise two-dimensional projections on an interactive dashboard, allowing selection criteria to be refined as the model and objectives evolve. The framework is showcased on a eight-dimensional in-silico fed-batch Chinese Hamster Ovary cell culture case study. We showed improved performance over BO when the expert has perfect domain knowledge; however, PFGS is not designed to outperform BO, but rather to present a HiL acquisition function framework.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Who Moved My $Z$ Boson? Revealing Resonance Features Inside a Neural Network
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Methods used in mechanistic interpretability have revealed human-aligned concepts inside language and image models. In this paper, we search for physics concepts inside a neural a generative collider physics model trained on real LHC data (ShellFlow). We discover features inside ShellFlow that represent resonances, such as the $Z$, $J/ψ$, and $Υ$. The network was never told which muons come from a resonance, it was only trained to generate the kinematics of the final-state particles. We use these features to alter aspects of the $Z$ boson: we change its mass between $\sim80$ and $105$ GeV, and removing such a feature from the neural network produces a broader $Z$ peak. In both cases the rest of the invariant mass spectrum remains mostly unchanged. The feature was built from the gradients of the neural network, and its selectivity was built using pattern recognition methods. A generative particle physics model trained on unlabeled data can be modified internally to change a physical quantity.
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: 10 pages (+4 pages of references, +14 pages of supplementary material, 29 total pages), 7 figures in the main text (+14 figures in the supplementary material, total of 21 pages)

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Towards Better Exploration in Sequential Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Test-time scaling improves language model reasoning by spending additional compute at inference. However, both classes of existing methods often fail to continue improving over long timescales. Parallel methods repeatedly sample independent answers from the model, scaling poorly on problems the model is unlikely to solve in a single attempt. In contrast, sequential methods build on previous answers to access new ideas, yet so far have not been shown to reach answers beyond those found by parallel scaling. First, we show that sequential scaling often stops improving because it becomes prematurely trapped in an attractor: a set of answers that prevents exploration of different answers once entered. Across 27 combinations of scaling methods, models, and benchmarks, we find that 53.8% of sequential scaling trajectories enter an attractor within four iterations. Second, we show that a simple model-mixing intervention helps escape attractors. This reduces the attractor hit rate by 21.2 percentage points on average, expands solution coverage beyond a compute-matched parallel baseline, and improves accuracy of recursive self-aggregation by at least 2.2 percentage points. Our results motivate refocusing long-horizon test-time scaling from parallel methods to sequential methods that improve previous answers.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: A Statistical Framework for Training Data Auditing of Large Language Models
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Training-data auditing asks whether data of interest were used to train a large language model (LLM), a question central to privacy auditing, copyright protection, and benchmark-contamination detection. These concerns are particularly relevant to the use of copyrighted books and scientific papers in pre-training, as well as synthetic text and medical question-answer records in fine-tuning. In practice, training membership signals may be concentrated in only a few passages of a long document, making it important to aggregate evidence within each document without diluting these localized signals. Beyond individual documents, auditing a target collection requires an overall assessment based on the document-level evidence. In this paper, we propose a unified statistical framework for document-level membership inference, target-collection global auditing, and suspicious-subset identification. We integrate complementary chunk-level membership evidence with Cauchy combination to construct document scores for document-level membership inference. The document scores and their calibrated p-values further enable an overall assessment of training-data collection use and the identification of suspicious documents through multiple testing. Under the stated exchangeability conditions, we establish finite-sample validity of document-level p-values, type-I error control for global auditing, and false discovery rate control for subset identification. Case studies on BookTection, Pile-arXiv, Cosmopedia, and HealthCareMagic demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework in auditing pre-training and fine-tuning data.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

LLM-agent benchmark for autonomous experimental design in digital twins of real labs (physics, chemistry, wet-lab biology, materials, engineering). 13 agents evaluated: Claude Fable 5.2 45.0, Opus 5.5 40.2, GPT-6.1-sol 31.7, plus DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and others

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Variational analysis of determinantal varieties
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Determinantal varieties---the sets of bounded-rank matrices or tensors---have attracted growing interest in low-rank optimization. The tangent cone to low-rank sets is widely studied and underpins a range of geometric methods. The second-order geometry, which encodes curvature information, is more intricate. In this work, we develop a unified framework to derive explicit formulas for both first- and second-order tangent sets to various low-rank sets, including low-rank matrices, tensors, symmetric matrices, and positive semidefinite matrices. The framework also accommodates the intersection of a low-rank set and another set satisfying some assumptions, thereby yielding a tangent intersection rule. Through the lens of tangent sets, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition under which a nonsmooth problem and its smooth parameterization share equivalent second-order stationary points. As applications, we exploit tangent sets to characterize optimality conditions for low-rank optimization and prove that verifying second-order optimality is NP-hard. Moreover, for low-rank semidefinite programs, the Burer--Monteiro parameterization maps fourth-order stationary points of the parameterized problem to second-order stationary points of the original problem. In a separate line of analysis, we investigate variational geometry of the graph of the normal cone to matrix varieties, deriving the explicit Bouligand tangent cone, Fréchet and Mordukhovich normal cones to the graph. These results are further applied to develop optimality conditions for low-rank bilevel programs.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because, without discounting, the span-contraction of the Bellman operator depends on the mixing properties of the underlying Markov dynamics. Whereas existing work typically assumes contraction, for instance through environment mixing, we study regularization toward a given reward-agnostic, $m$-step mixing policy to control the mixing properties of the learned policy. Our central mixing lemma quantifies how the reference policy's mixing properties transfer to the resulting learned policies. In particular, a single regularizer-dependent quantity simultaneously controls the contraction of the regularized Bellman operator and the exploration of the resulting policies. A second regularizer-dependent quantity controls the bias introduced by regularization, revealing a trade-off between convergence speed and approximation accuracy. Building on this result, we establish finite-time guarantees for regularized $Q$-iteration, synchronous and single-trajectory $Q$-learning, and $Q$-planning. Under one-step mixing, our bounds for approximating the regularized fixed point match the classical model-query bound for relative value iteration and, up to logarithmic factors, an existing sample-complexity bound for synchronous $Q$-learning. We also establish finite-time guarantees under multi-step mixing. For $Q$-planning, we characterize how the planning horizon trades off boundary bias against sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, with larger benefits under more severe bottlenecks; and (ii) the observed rankings of $α$-divergence regularizers by bias and convergence speed are consistent with our theoretical analysis.
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: 10 pages main body, 58 pages references and appendix, 11 figures. Under review

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing remains challenging because experimental datasets are limited and process-property relationships vary across materials and operating conditions. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) govern process stability and defect formation. Conventional ML models typically use dimensional process parameters, which represent laser-material interactions only implicitly and may limit cross-material transfer. This study evaluates whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, combining laser processing conditions with material thermophysical properties, improve melt pool prediction over raw process parameters. We systematically benchmark seven models: four classical ML methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2). Experiments span 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets, covering regression of melt pool width and depth and classification of melting modes. Dimensionless features yield comparable or superior predictive performance in most settings, with the largest gains in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). Tabular foundation models generally achieve stronger classification performance than classical baselines, particularly for multi-material datasets. These findings indicate that combining physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular models can improve data-efficient melt pool modeling and support more transferable process-window identification in LPBF.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Learning Multinomial Logits in $O(n \log n)$ time
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: A Multinomial Logit (MNL) model is composed of a finite universe of items $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, each assigned a positive weight. A query specifies an admissible subset---called a slate---and the model chooses one item from that slate with probability proportional to its weight. This query model is also known as the Plackett--Luce model or conditional sampling oracle in the literature. Although MNLs have been studied extensively, a basic computational question remains open: given query access to slates, how efficiently can we learn weights so that, for every slate, the induced choice distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the ground truth? This question is central to MNL learning and has direct implications for modern recommender system interfaces. We provide both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms for this task. Our first adaptive algorithm makes $O(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ queries and learns every choice distribution in total variation distance $\varepsilon$. We also provide a second adaptive algorithm that with $O(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ queries provides a stronger guarantee: each choice distribution is approximated to a multiplicative $1\pm\varepsilon$ error (except for subsets of mass smaller than $\varepsilon$). We complement these algorithms with lower bounds of $Ω(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ for total variation distance and $Ω(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ for the multiplicative error guarantee, showing the optimality of our adaptive algorithms. Our non-adaptive algorithm makes $O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}\log n \log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)$ queries to obtain guarantees under the multiplicative error notion. We complement this result with an $Ω(\frac{n^2 \log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ lower bound for any non-adaptive algorithm, showing that our algorithm is almost tight in $n$ (within a $\log n$ factor).
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: We prove two new results. In particular, we provide a $O(n \log n / \varepsilon^2)$ algorithm for learning in $d_1$ error, which closes one of the main questions left open in the previous versions of the paper

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: OpenTME: An Open Dataset of AI-powered H&E Tumor Microenvironment Profiles from TCGA
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a central role in cancer progression, treatment response, and patient outcomes, yet large-scale, consistent, and quantitative TME characterization from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathology remains scarce. We introduce OpenTME, an open-access dataset of pre-computed TME profiles derived from 5,268 H&E-stained whole-slide images across ten cancer types (bladder, breast, colorectal, head and neck, liver, lung, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, and stomach cancer) from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). All outputs were generated using HETA (H&E Tissue Analysis), an AI-powered application built on the Atlas family of pathology foundation models, which performs tissue quality control, tissue segmentation, cell detection and classification, tumor zone and tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) detection, and spatial neighborhood analysis, yielding over 20,000 quantitative readouts per slide at cell-level resolution, including curated features such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, tumor mitotic index, or mature TLS counts. OpenTME is available for non-commercial academic research on Hugging Face. We will continue to expand OpenTME over time and anticipate it will serve as a resource for biomarker discovery, spatial biology research, and the development of computational methods for TME analysis.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. How does the safety effect of a single activation edit vary across early reasoning states, and what factors govern that variation? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, site-specific edits concentrate safety gains in the opening CoT tokens. Norm-matched controls on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (8B) disentangle two factors behind this curve: holding an effective direction and edit budget fixed still yields much larger early ($t_1$-$t_5$) than later ($t_6$-$t_8$) gains, whereas the near-zero site-specific $t_3$ gain reflects higher optimisation variance despite rising risk-probe AUROC. Forced prefixes shift the high-gain region with the opening context, and a four-arm intervention shows that ~98% of the net gain at $t_2$ propagates through the changed next token. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function Across Architectures
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this complementary form of transfer through a learn-freeze-transfer protocol, in which the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run, and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activation represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures (standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Invertible Transport Between Sample-Only Distributions via Projected Characteristic Functions
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary:
Many useful latent distributions can be sampled but do not have a tractable density. Such distributions may be represented by empirical collections of real-world observations or generated by scientific simulators and black-box generative models. These sample-only priors cannot be used directly in likelihood-based normalizing flows, which require evaluating the prior density. We propose Projected Characteristic-Function matching (PCF), a density-free framework for learning an invertible map between a data distribution and a prior specified only through samples.
  Our method aligns distributions using projected empirical characteristic functions, eliminating the need for density estimation, adversarial training, or paired observations. To address the non-uniqueness of the transport map, we introduce an optional transport regularizer that selects lower-displacement transformations while preserving endpoint alignment.
  We benchmark PCF on controlled transports, sample-efficiency studies, and high-dimensional alignment tasks. PCF matches the accuracy of kernel MMD on the controlled benchmark and on raw-pixel MNIST--USPS at a cost linear in the batch size, and it is more sample-efficient, achieving lower endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs across library sizes. By avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation, it reduces discrepancy memory by 29.8% and trains at batch sizes where kernel MMD exceeds GPU memory. These results show that PCF provides accurate and efficient invertible transport, particularly in sample- and memory-limited settings.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: 33 pages (15 pages main text and 18 pages Supplementary Information), 4 figures

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks for a Universal Fluid Gibbs Free Energy Equation of State
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Over the past three centuries, many thermodynamics researchers have worked to develop fluid equations of state with both high accuracy and broad applicability, proposing various theoretical frameworks and models. Building on these efforts, this study uses Gibbs free energy as the starting point and introduces thermodynamically consistent neural networks to construct a fluid equation of state based on Gibbs free energy (GEoS). This approach establishes a novel machine learning framework that provides a unified representation of fluid states. GEoS performs well on the vapor- and liquid-phase density test sets, with average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25% and 3.96%, respectively. It outperforms conventional volume-translated cubic equations of state and existing machine learning models, demonstrating its effectiveness. Further analysis using the UMAP dimensionality reduction method shows that most molecules in the test set belong to extrapolation systems, confirming the strong generalization ability of the model. Finally, the test results show that the PC-SAFT equation fitted using GEoS maintains high predictive accuracy, providing a reliable basis for its practical application in industry.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Learning with Local Search MCMC Layers
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Integrating combinatorial optimization layers into neural networks has recently attracted significant research interest. However, many existing approaches lack theoretical guarantees or fail to perform adequately when relying on inexact solvers. This is a critical limitation, as many operations research problems are NP-hard, often necessitating the use of neighborhood-based local search heuristics. In this paper, we introduce a principled approach for learning with such inexact solvers. Inspired by the connection between simulated annealing and Metropolis-Hastings, we transform the problem specific neighborhood systems used in local search heuristics into proposal distributions, implementing MCMC on the set of feasible solutions. This allows us to construct differentiable, stochastic combinatorial layers and associated loss functions. Replacing an exact solver with a local search strongly reduces the computational burden of learning on many applications. We demonstrate our approach on a dynamic vehicle routing problem with time windows, binary vector and k-subset prediction tasks, as well as a multi-dimensional knapsack decision-focused learning problem.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: SpikingGamma: Temporally Precise Online SNN Training Through Smoothed Temporal Delays
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Neuromorphic hardware implementations of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, low-latency AI through sparse, event-driven computation. Yet, training SNNs under fine temporal discretization remains challenging, hindering low-latency responsiveness and the mapping of software-trained SNNs to efficient hardware. In current approaches, spiking neurons are modeled as self-recurrent units, embedded into recurrent networks to maintain state over time, and trained with BPTT or RTRL variants based on surrogate gradients. These methods scale poorly with temporal resolution, while online approximations exhibit instability for long sequences and tend to fail at capturing temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we develop SpikingGamma, an SNN architecture in which neurons maintain a compact bank of smoothed-delay states and communicate through sigma-delta spike-coding. We show that in feedforward networks, SpikingGamma supports direct online error backpropagation through the continuous reconstruction signal, avoiding surrogate gradients through the spike discontinuity. This enables stable learning of temporal patterns with minimal spiking and scales feedforward SNNs to complex tasks and benchmarks with competitive accuracy, all while remaining robust to the temporal resolution of the model. Our approach offers both an alternative to recurrent SNNs trained with surrogate gradients, and a novel route for mapping SNNs to neuromorphic hardware.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: SCAR: State-Space Compression for AI-Based Radio Resource Management of Vehicular Services
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: The increasing demand for connected vehicular services poses significant challenges for AI-based network and service management due to the high volume and rapid variability of network state information. Traditional management and control mechanisms struggle to scale when processing fine-grained metrics such as Channel Quality Indicators (CQIs) in dynamic vehicular environments. To address this challenge, we propose SCAR (State-Space Compression for AI-Based Radio Resource Management), an edge-assisted framework that abstracts high-dimensional CQI information into compact representations for AI-based management. SCAR employs machine-learning (ML)-based compression techniques, including clustering and radial basis function (RBF) networks, to reduce the dimensionality of CQI-derived state information while preserving essential features relevant to management decisions. The resulting compressed states are used to train reinforcement learning (RL)-based management policies that dynamically adapt the throughput-fairness trade-off according to service-level fairness objectives defined by the NGMN. Simulation results show that CQI compression improves average NGMN feasible-region occupancy from 56.32% to 88.07% across ten RL algorithms, reaching 97.76% for the best-performing RL configuration, with limited throughput degradation and competitive computational overhead. Furthermore, simulated annealing with stochastic tunneling (SAST)-based clustering reduces state compression distortion by approximately 10% compared with conventional K-means clustering. These results demonstrate SCAR's ability to provide compact state representations for RL-based network and service management while improving service-level fairness in dynamic vehicular systems.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Loss-Guided Tsetlin Machines: Making the Learning Objective Explicit
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: The Tsetlin Machine (TM) has no explicit notion of a loss function. Its learning signal is fixed to an implicit, margin-based update rule (MBUR), with no way to choose an objective function suited to a specific task. This paper introduces Loss-Guided TM, which replaces MBUR with an explicit and swappable loss function. In our proposed method, clause feedback and weight updates are driven by the loss, while keeping the Tsetlin Automaton and clause logic unchanged. The approach incorporates cross entropy (CE), symmetric cross entropy (SCE), and asymmetric loss (ASL). We evaluate Loss-Guided TM across six datasets that span multiclass, multilabel, and binary classification tasks. With a suitable loss, Loss-Guided TM matches or improves accuracy and F1 over MBUR on five of the six datasets. The gains are greatest for the imbalanced multilabel datasets, where ASL improves macro F1 by up to 9 percentage points. With CE, Loss-Guided TM is also significantly better calibrated than MBUR on all six datasets, reducing calibration error by a factor of 3 to 11. A qualitative inspection shows that the clause-based global interpretability, examined at the per-class level on image and text data, is preserved when using the Loss-Guided mechanism. These results show that our explicit TM learning objective allows direct targeting of uncertainty calibration, data imbalance, and task structure, opening the TM to the broader literature on loss functions.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: The Alignment Tax Is Graded: Task-Selective Capability Loss Under Length-Normalized DPO with SFT Retention
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Setting. This is an empirical characterization study; we propose no new method and run no comparisons against alternative objectives. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA and length-normalized DPO plus an SFT retention term (the RPO objective) on structured financial-filing tasks, and track downstream capability as the implicit reward margin grows to $\sim 7$ $β$-scaled units (nf4 training; $\sim 3$ under fp16 measurement on the unquantized base). Question. Does margin growth degrade capability uniformly across tasks, or selectively? Findings. In a pre-registered study (8 seeds, 6 unseen at freeze) with artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing, the alignment tax is graded and task-selective: extraction is preserved ($Δ= -0.55$ pts, equivalent at $\pm5$ pts), json loses little ($Δ= -3.52$ pts, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely ($Δ= -30$ pts). Router's loss concentrates in a margin 1-3 damage window containing a transient format-break spike. The margin is accounted for almost entirely ($\geq 96\%$) by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward approximately flat, consistent with the retention term anchoring it; we do not attribute the behavioral damage to any single gradient channel. Gold-logp deflation is task-selective (extraction $-0.15$, json $-1.04$, router $-1.47$ nats/token under fp16), with gold selectively protected relative to incorrect controls on extraction (8/8 seeds). QLoRA reward margins differ up to $3.4\times$ between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement, with an axis-dependent gap. Scope. Length-normalized rewards with SFT retention, sparse LoRA on 8/32 layers, one 4B model, easily-separable synthetic preferences, three structured tasks. A no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: 13 pages (incl. cover page), 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. Please cite the published version (DOI: 10.1109/TBME.2026.3666306). Code: https://github.com/Stef-Martin/E2E-MRE

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: How Network Topology and Data Heterogeneity Shape Decentralized Learning: A Spectral Analysis
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Network topology influences decentralized federated learning through information mixing and the relative contribution of individual nodes. While existing analyses primarily focus on spectral mixing properties, they often assume doubly stochastic aggregation, overlooking topology-dependent influence under irregular communication networks. We develop a spectral framework that separates two complementary mechanisms: the dominant eigenmode determines the consensus trajectory and node influence, while non-dominant eigenmodes govern the propagation and attenuation of disagreement. Under uniform neighborhood averaging, we show that the stationary influence is proportional to node degree plus one and derive a bound relating model disagreement to spectral mixing and gradient heterogeneity. We then investigate how these mechanisms interact with the data distribution across nodes. Experiments across regular and heterogeneous network topologies reveal nearly identical learning dynamics under IID data, while network size and connectivity affect how unevenly distributed information is learned under non-IID data. For non-IID settings, we characterize how the distribution of data across nodes shapes the relative contribution of local information to consensus dynamics.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: FlexTSF: A Flexible Forecasting Model for Time Series with Variable Regularities
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Generalizing across time series with irregular temporal structures poses a persistent challenge for universal time series forecasting models. Existing approaches often assume regular sampling or depend heavily on imputation, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where irregularities are prevalent due to diverse sensing devices and recording practices. To address this gap, we propose FlexTSF, a flexible and domain-adaptive forecasting model specifically designed for time series with variable temporal regularities. At its foundation lies the IVP Patcher, a continuous-time patching module leveraging Initial Value Problems (IVPs) to inherently handle uneven sampling intervals, variable sequence lengths, and missing values. Built upon a decoder-only Transformer architecture, FlexTSF integrates normalized timestamp inputs and domain-specific statistical descriptors through a specialized causal self-attention mechanism, enabling adaptability across domains. Extensive experiments on 16 datasets demonstrate FlexTSF's effectiveness, significantly outperforming existing models in classic forecasting scenarios, zero-shot generalization, and low-resource fine-tuning conditions.
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: Published in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of 2026 IEEE 8th International Conference on Robotics, Intelligent Control and Artificial Intelligence(IEEE-RICAI 2026); proceedings not yet published

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Learning to Compare Neural Representations from Parameterized Computation Graphs
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Comparing internal representations across trained models is important for identifying corresponding layers and selecting components for model reuse. Yet, direct comparisons at inference require evaluating candidate models on known reference inputs and collecting their internal activations. In this paper, we study whether internal representation similarity measured across independently trained models can instead be learned to predict in unseen models from their parameterized computations. We introduce a framework that applies a graph metanetwork for mapping each internal site to an embedding derived from its upstream computations while accounting for hidden-coordinate permutation and internal attention-basis transformations. We analyze the structural properties of our estimators and derive conditional guarantees for layer retrieval and stitching candidate selection. Empirically, we find that the learned predictors support relation estimation and low-regret layer retrieval. They also select useful stitching connections while not being trained on stitching outcomes. This opens up a new way to study representation similarity directly from trained neural networks: representational relations learned across a collection of trained models can generalize to new computations, and that the predicted relations can guide candidate selection before direct measurement or adapter fitting for functional evaluations.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select. Those switches can alter the answer scores in ways that derivatives do not capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these extra effects, then adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, our method reduces the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60\% on Qwen3.6 and 47\% on Gemma4, relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Xaurora: Generative Weather Forecasting with Denoising Stochastic Interpolants from a Foundation Model Prior
Machine Learning / Foundation Models.summary: Deep learning has revolutionised weather forecasting in recent years, especially through atmospheric foundation models, which offer competitive skill for a fraction of the computational costs of classic physics-based models. However, most existing foundation models are deterministic, limiting the generation of large ensembles for accurate uncertainty quantification, extreme weather risk assessment, and long-range weather forecasting. Furthermore, these models incur a large, often prohibitive, computational overhead to train from scratch. To address these shortcomings, we turn a pretrained deterministic prior model, namely the Aurora foundation model, into a generative ensemble-prediction model. To that end, we introduce a novel generative method, Denoising Stochastic Interpolants, combined with a replay buffer for Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) rollout, enabling probabilistic training of SDE trajectories. Our stochastic foundation model, Xaurora, is finetuned from the small Aurora version, yet it approaches the state-of-the-art on global ensemble metrics and is competitive with the large version of Aurora. Our method is parameter and sample efficient, and generates skilful 15-day forecasts in 7 minutes. Our results demonstrate that deterministic foundation models can be efficiently extended into even stronger stochastic models.

Machine Learning / Foundation Models.title: Iterative Scarcity-Guided Exploration: Bootstrapping Generative Auto-bidding from Narrow Support
